```{r setup, include=FALSE}
knitr::opts_chunk$set(echo = TRUE)
# Bash chunks are a record of commands you ran in the Terminal. Knitting shows
# them but doesn't run them again.
knitr::opts_hooks$set(engine = function(options) {
  if (options$engine == "bash") options$eval <- FALSE
  options
})
```

this chunk above is running on R, but it will not run all the bash chunks in the document. to not have a bash chunk run everytime, you also do {bash, eval=FALSE} or just remove the {} in bash chunk so now R thinks it is a R chunk and will not run it. 
Notes for [Workshop 2](https://mb5370.bioinformatics.guide/workshop2.html). Run the commands for this workshop in the Terminal, from inside the folder named under each heading. Copy each command you run into a bash chunk.

## Redbean assembly

Commands run in `redbean/`.
```{bash}
cd ~/mb5370-workshops/redbean
```

- collecting a small subset data for the initial assembly
- will be using the first 3 files equating to 12000 reads and around 6x coverage of the target genome
- will not be enough to generate a good assembly

```{bash}
cat /pvol/data/amtp4/*_[012].fastq > amtp4.fastq
```

- running the assembly 
```{bash}
wtdbg2 -x ont -g 5m -t 4 -i amtp4.fastq -fo amtp4
wtpoa-cns -t 4 -i amtp4.ctg.lay.gz -fo amtp4.ctg.fa
```

- bins = binary

the wtdbg2 is quick but very long
the wtpoa-cns takes 70 secs but very short text

- inspecting the assembly statistics
```{bash}
assembly-stats amtp4.ctg.fa
```
 - assembly looks more compact and easier to read as it says the sum, number of entries, average and the largest number, there is also no gaps
 
- redoing the assembly using a better coverage depth - using data equivalent to approx. 20x coverage

```{bash}
cat /pvol/data/amtp4/*.fastq > amtp4_20x.fastq
wtdbg2 -x ont -g 5m -t 4 -i amtp4_20x.fastq -fo amtp4_20x
wtpoa-cns -t 4 -i amtp4_20x.ctg.lay.gz -fo amtp4_20x.ctg.fa
```

amtp4 - low coverage
amtp2_20x - hogh coverage
